entries.title: Finding the Next in a Sequence
entries.summary: Look for what changes each time.
entries.body: In a sequence, each step follows the same rule. 2, 4, 6, 8 comes from adding 2 each time. When you cannot see the rule, try the next few numbers - sometimes the rule is only clear later.
facts: Each step in a sequence follows a rule.
Sometimes you need to write a few more terms to see the pattern.

entries.title: The Odd One Out
entries.body: When three things share a feature and one does not, that one is the odd one out. A square, a circle and a triangle are all shapes, but a square and a triangle have corners and a circle does not.
facts: The odd one out breaks the shared rule.
Look for the feature most of them share.
There can be more than one good answer if you explain it.

entries.title: Sorting
entries.body: Sorting is one of the most useful thinking skills. You can sort by colour, size, shape, sound or any rule you choose. Good sorters often notice that a thing can fit in more than one group.
facts: Sorting uses a rule you choose.
The same object can belong to more than one group.

entries.title: Solving Clues
entries.summary: Good clues let you work out an answer.
entries.body: When a puzzle gives you clues, write down what you know and cross things out as you find them out. A clue like 'it is not red and it is taller than the box' is two clues in one sentence.
facts: Write down what you know as you go.
Some clues have two parts in them.
Look for clues that rule things out.

entries.title: Thinking Sideways
entries.summary: Sometimes the answer needs a new idea.
entries.body: Some puzzles cannot be solved by thinking in the usual way. You have to look at the problem from a different angle. Asking 'why' instead of 'how' is often the key.
facts: Sideways thinking means looking at the problem differently.
Asking why can unlock a stuck puzzle.
Different ideas can all lead to a good answer.

entries.title: Planning
entries.body: Before you start a job, think about the steps. What has to be done first? What could go wrong? Planning a trip, a game or a piece of work makes it go more smoothly.
facts: Plan the steps before you start.
Think about what could go wrong and be ready.
A plan can be changed as you learn more.

questions.explanation: The rule is adding 2 each time, so the next number is 10.
Odd numbers go up by 2, so the next is 9.

questions.prompt: Which is the odd one out: square, circle, triangle?
questions.explanation: A circle has no corners while the others do.
Sorting means grouping things using a rule you choose.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when solving a clue puzzle?
questions.explanation: Writing down the facts helps you spot what is left.

options: Looking at a problem from a different angle
questions.explanation: Sideways thinking means finding a new angle on the problem.

questions.prompt: Which question often unlocks a stuck puzzle?
questions.explanation: Asking why gets to the heart of the problem.

questions.prompt: Why plan before starting a job?
questions.explanation: A plan means fewer mistakes and less time wasted.

questions.prompt: One object can belong to more than one group when sorting.
questions.explanation: You can sort by colour and also by size at the same time.
The rule is adding 5 each time, so the next is 25.
